<div class="page-shell">
  <header class="page-intro">
    <h1>Research</h1>
    <p class="page-lede">
      Selected work across theoretical neuroscience, large-scale brain
      dynamics, and biologically inspired learning.
    </p>
  </header>

  <section class="page-section research-collection" aria-labelledby="research-list-heading">
    <p class="page-section__label" id="research-list-heading">Selected work</p>
    <div class="page-section__body research-list">
      <article class="research-item">
        <div class="research-item__media" role="img" aria-label="Reserved image area for Serial Dependence in Visual Working Memory">
          <span class="research-item__media-number">01</span>
          <span class="research-item__media-label">Image / Figure</span>
        </div>
        <div class="research-item__content">
          <p class="research-item__type">Graduate Summer Research</p>
          <h2>Serial Dependence in Visual Working Memory</h2>
          <p class="research-item__context">
            <span>New York University Shanghai</span>
            <span>Jun–Aug 2026</span>
          </p>
          <p class="research-item__advisor">Advisor: Sukbin Lim</p>
          <div class="research-item__copy">
            <p>
              I studied how recent and more distant experiences shape current
              visual working-memory representations. I developed a computational
              model combining history-dependent efficient coding with
              attractor-based memory to investigate the coexistence of attractive
              and repulsive serial biases across different timescales.
            </p>
            <p>
              The model qualitatively reproduced short-term attraction and
              longer-range repulsion under short-delay conditions, while
              delay-dependent discrepancies motivated further exploration of
              multiscale history effects and memory uncertainty.
            </p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="research-item">
        <div class="research-item__media" role="img" aria-label="Reserved image area for Large-Scale Network Dynamics during Working Memory">
          <span class="research-item__media-number">02</span>
          <span class="research-item__media-label">Image / Figure</span>
        </div>
        <div class="research-item__content">
          <p class="research-item__type">Research Project</p>
          <h2>Large-Scale Network Dynamics during Working Memory</h2>
          <p class="research-item__context">
            <span>Westlake University</span>
            <span>Apr 2025–May 2026</span>
          </p>
          <p class="research-item__advisor">Advisor: Yuchen Xiao</p>
          <div class="research-item__copy">
            <p>
              I investigated how distributed brain networks coordinate during
              working-memory recognition, encoding, and retrieval using
              intracranial recordings from 1,652 sites across 36 patients.
            </p>
            <p>
              I analyzed cross-frequency coupling and directed information flow
              to characterize large-scale interactions across different stages of
              working memory. My primary contribution was developing and applying
              a time-delay embedded hidden Markov model (TDE-HMM) to identify
              time-resolved latent network states and characterize their dynamics
              during working-memory processing. This work contributed to a
              bioRxiv preprint on frontotemporal network dynamics during
              working-memory processing.
            </p>
          </div>
          <a
            class="research-item__link"
            href="https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.23.740204"
            target="_blank"
            rel="noopener noreferrer"
          >View preprint <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></a>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="research-item">
        <div class="research-item__media" role="img" aria-label="Reserved image area for Multiscale Dynamics of Functional Ultrasound Hemodynamics">
          <span class="research-item__media-number">03</span>
          <span class="research-item__media-label">Image / Figure</span>
        </div>
        <div class="research-item__content">
          <p class="research-item__type">Undergraduate Thesis</p>
          <h2>Multiscale Dynamics of Functional Ultrasound Hemodynamics</h2>
          <p class="research-item__context">
            <span>Xi'an Jiaotong University</span>
            <span>Jan–Jun 2026</span>
          </p>
          <p class="research-item__advisor">Advisors: Junjie Jiang and Zhiqiang Wei</p>
          <div class="research-item__copy">
            <p>
              For my undergraduate thesis, I studied multiscale hemodynamic
              changes in a rat neuroinflammation dataset using functional
              ultrasound imaging. I characterized changes in spectral activity,
              functional connectivity, long-range temporal dependence, and
              low-dimensional network structure across experimental conditions.
            </p>
            <p>
              I further developed a delayed coupled-oscillator model with a
              vascular observation layer and used approximate Bayesian computation
              to relate changes in observed hemodynamics to interpretable
              dynamical parameters.
            </p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="research-item">
        <div class="research-item__media" role="img" aria-label="Reserved image area for Biologically Inspired Learning for Monocular Depth Estimation">
          <span class="research-item__media-number">04</span>
          <span class="research-item__media-label">Image / Figure</span>
        </div>
        <div class="research-item__content">
          <p class="research-item__type">Independent Research</p>
          <h2>Biologically Inspired Learning for Monocular Depth Estimation</h2>
          <p class="research-item__context">
            <span>Jun–Oct 2024</span>
          </p>
          <div class="research-item__copy">
            <p>
              I explored whether biologically inspired Hebbian learning could be
              incorporated into modern computer-vision architectures. I developed
              a hybrid ResNet–U-Net model with a SoftHebb layer that adapted
              intermediate feature representations through co-activation-based
              updates for monocular depth estimation.
            </p>
            <p>
              This work resulted in my first research publication and helped shape
              my later interest in the relationship between biological and
              artificial learning.
            </p>
          </div>
          <a
            class="research-item__link"
            href="https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/82/20241264"
            target="_blank"
            rel="noopener noreferrer"
          >View publication <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></a>
        </div>
      </article>
    </div>
  </section>
